lead: Every structure has preferred frequencies, called natural frequencies. A wing, a tailplane or a panel pushed and released will oscillate at these frequencies, and damping decides how quickly the motion dies out. In flight, aerodynamic forces can feed energy back into the motion. That coupling is aeroelasticity. It matters because a wing can twist too far at one speed, called divergence, or oscillate with growing amplitude at another, called flutter. Both are certification issues. This chapter builds the one-degree-of-freedom vibration model, then uses it to explain divergence, flutter and reduced frequency in plain terms.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 energy methods for generalized mass and stiffness, and 6.7 for how fibre direction sets stiffness.

sections.h3: One degree of freedom: mass, spring and dashpot

blocks.text: Take a single mass m (kg) on a spring of stiffness k (N/m), with a dashpot of damping c (N·s/m). Let x(t) be displacement in metres. The equation of motion is m (d²x/dt²) + c (dx/dt) + k x = F(t). With no force and no damping, the mass oscillates freely.

blocks.where: ω<sub>n</sub> is the undamped natural frequency in rad/s; k is stiffness in N/m; m is mass in kg; f<sub>n</sub> is the same frequency in Hz. The 2π converts rad/s to Hz.

blocks.text: Damping is measured by the damping ratio ζ, a pure number. Critical damping is c<sub>c</sub> = 2√(km). Aircraft structures are lightly damped: ζ is often a few percent. ζ < 1 is underdamped (the mass oscillates as it dies away), ζ = 1 is critically damped (fastest return with no overshoot), and ζ > 1 is overdamped (slow return, no oscillation).

blocks.where: ζ is the damping ratio; c is the dashpot constant in N·s/m; k is stiffness in N/m; m is mass in kg.

blocks.text: For a harmonic force F<sub>0</sub> sin(Ωt), let r = Ω/ω<sub>n</sub> be the frequency ratio. The steady vibration amplitude is largest near r = 1. This is resonance. Damping limits the peak.

blocks.where: X is amplitude in metres; F<sub>0</sub> is force amplitude in N; k is stiffness in N/m; r = Ω/ω<sub>n</sub> is frequency ratio; ζ is damping ratio. At r = 1, X = F<sub>0</sub>/(2ζk).

sections.h3: Modes and lumped models of real structures

blocks.text: A real wing has many masses and stiffnesses, so it has many natural frequencies. Each natural frequency has a mode shape: a shape in which all points move sinusoidally at the same frequency. The first bending mode, the first torsion mode and higher modes each have their own frequency and damping.

For hand calculations, replace the continuous structure by one generalized coordinate q(t). Choose a trial mode shape φ(x), then compute a generalized mass M and generalized stiffness K. The same one-degree-of-freedom formula applies.

items: Choose a mode shape φ(x) that satisfies the end conditions and is normalized, for example φ = 1 at the tip.
Compute generalized mass M = ∫ m(x) φ² dx over the length.
Compute generalized stiffness K = ∫ EI(x) (d²φ/dx²)² dx for bending, adding torsion stiffness terms if the mode twists.
Estimate the natural frequency from ω<sub>n</sub> = √(K/M).

blocks.text: This is the Rayleigh quotient from energy methods. It gives an upper estimate of the true fundamental frequency when φ is a reasonable guess. Composite stiffness from 6.8 enters K, so a softer laminate lowers the frequency.

Aeroelasticity is the feedback between structural motion and aerodynamic force. Static divergence is a torsional instability. Airloads twist a wing; the twist changes the airloads. At a high enough speed, the aerodynamic pitching moment slope equals the elastic torsional stiffness, so any small twist grows without oscillation.

blocks.where: q<sub>D</sub> is divergence dynamic pressure in N/m²; K<sub>θ</sub> is torsional stiffness in N·m/rad; S is reference area in m²; c is chord in m; C<sub>mα</sub> is pitching moment slope per radian; V<sub>D</sub> is divergence speed in m/s; ρ is air density in kg/m³.

blocks.text: C<sub>mα</sub> is negative for a stable section. The formula uses magnitudes, so write q<sub>D</sub> = K<sub>θ</sub>/(S c |C<sub>mα</sub>|) and V<sub>D</sub> = √(2q<sub>D</sub>/ρ).

Flutter is dynamic. Bending and torsion couple through unsteady airloads. At the flutter speed, the net aerodynamic damping becomes negative and an oscillation grows. Flutter can occur below divergence, so both must be checked.

Unsteady aerodynamics depends on how fast the wing oscillates compared with the airflow. That ratio is the reduced frequency k<sub>r</sub> = ω b/V. Here b is a reference semi-chord in m, ω is oscillation frequency in rad/s, and V is true airspeed in m/s. Small k<sub>r</sub> means quasi-steady flow; large k<sub>r</sub> means aerodynamic lag matters.

figure.caption: Resonance peak at r = 1; damping limits the amplitude. The curve uses ζ = 0.2, so the peak is 1/(2ζ) = 2.5 times the static amplitude.

spec.aria: Plot of vibration amplitude against frequency ratio for damping ratio 0.2.

examples.question: A wing model has mass m = 500 kg and stiffness k = 200 kN/m. Find its natural frequency in rad/s and in Hz. With damping c = 4000 N·s/m, find the damping ratio ζ.
steps: Convert to Hz: f<sub>n</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>/(2π) = 20/(2π) = 3.18 Hz.
examples.answer: ω<sub>n</sub> = 20 rad/s, f<sub>n</sub> = 3.18 Hz, and ζ = 0.20.
examples.check:
import math
m = 500.0
k = 200000.0
c = 4000.0
wn = math.sqrt(k/m)
fn = wn/(2.0*math.pi)
zeta = c/(2.0*math.sqrt(k*m))
print(round(wn, 2))
print(round(fn, 2))
print(round(zeta, 2))

traps: Reporting ω<sub>n</sub> in rad/s as f<sub>n</sub> in Hz without dividing by 2π: 20 rad/s is 3.18 Hz, not 20 Hz.
Using ζ = c/√(km) or forgetting the 2: critical damping is c<sub>c</sub> = 2√(km), so ζ = c/(2√(km)).
Calling static divergence flutter: divergence is a non-oscillatory loss of static torsional stiffness; flutter is a growing oscillation.
Mixing the two k symbols: spring stiffness k is in N/m; reduced frequency k<sub>r</sub> = ωb/V is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Define natural frequency and damping ratio for a one-degree-of-freedom system. Give both formulas.
quiz.a: Natural frequency ω<sub>n</sub> = √(k/m) is the radian frequency of free undamped oscillation. Damping ratio ζ = c/(2√(km)) compares the dashpot constant c with critical damping 2√(km).

quiz.q: Why does damping reduce the resonance peak strongly but change the natural frequency only slightly when ζ is small?
quiz.a: Damping adds a force proportional to velocity, removing energy each cycle. Near resonance the response is large, so the damping term is a large fraction of the force. Away from resonance, inertia and stiffness terms dominate. For small ζ, peak height changes roughly as 1/(2ζ), while peak frequency changes only by a factor near √(1 − 2ζ²).

quiz.q: A mass m = 200 kg is on a spring k = 80 kN/m. Find ω<sub>n</sub> and f<sub>n</sub>.
For the same m = 200 kg and k = 80 kN/m, the damping is c = 1600 N·s/m. Find ζ.
Explain the difference between static divergence and flutter. Which one is an oscillation?
quiz.a: Divergence is static: at q<sub>D</sub> the aerodynamic pitching moment slope equals the elastic torsional stiffness, so any twist grows without oscillation. Flutter is dynamic: bending and torsion couple through unsteady airloads, and a growing oscillation appears when net aerodynamic damping is negative. Flutter is the oscillation; divergence is not.

quiz.q: A wing oscillates at ω = 30 rad/s. The reference semi-chord is b = 1.5 m and true airspeed is V = 150 m/s. Find the reduced frequency k<sub>r</sub>.
Why do lumped models use generalized mass and stiffness instead of every point mass and spring?
quiz.a: A real wing has many degrees of freedom. A mode shape lets us replace distributed mass and stiffness by one generalized mass M and one generalized stiffness K. Then ω = √(K/M). The first few modes usually carry most of the response, so a small model is enough for a hand estimate.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, flutter clearance uses unsteady aerodynamic panel methods, wind-tunnel aeroelastic models and flight flutter tests. Composite wings need the stiffness coupling from laminate theory because bending–torsion coupling can lower flutter speed. Search next for the p-k method, reduced frequency, and ground vibration testing.
